turns.q: Is Amazon's earnings quality deteriorating? Put operating cash flow beside net income for the last eight quarters, show the accruals ratio trend, tell me whether receivables and inventory are growing faster than revenue over the same windows, and say what that means for the size of our AMZN position.
turns.answer:
## Bottom line
Amazon’s earnings quality shows a **recent deterioration signal, but not yet a sustained decline**. The latest quarter combines weaker cash conversion, a mildly positive accruals ratio, and sharply faster receivables growth. However, the preceding quarter was exceptionally cash-generative, inventory growth has improved, and the eight-quarter history remains broadly cash-backed.
## Cash flow versus earnings
| Quarter end | Operating cash flow | Net income | Cash conversion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024-06-30 | $25.28B | $13.48B | 187.5% |
| 2024-09-30 | $25.97B | $15.33B | 169.4% |
| 2024-12-31 | $45.64B | $20.00B | 228.1% |
| 2025-03-31 | $17.02B | $17.13B | 99.3% |
| 2025-06-30 | $32.52B | $18.16B | 179.0% |
| 2025-09-30 | $35.52B | $21.19B | 167.7% |
| 2025-12-31 | $54.46B | $21.19B | 257.0% |
| 2026-03-31 | $26.03B | $30.25B | 86.0% |
Cash exceeded earnings in most quarters. The concern is that the latest conversion dropped below full coverage, versus 99.3% in the same quarter a year earlier. Quarterly cash flow is seasonal, so the latest reading should not be extrapolated alone.
## Accruals trend
The sequence was:
- -2.13%
- -1.82%
- -4.10%
- 0.02%
- -2.10%
- -1.97%
- -4.07%
- 0.46%
The pattern is seasonal and broadly stable across like quarters, but the latest 0.46% is less favorable than 0.02%. That supports a deterioration flag, though its small magnitude does not indicate a broad accrual problem by itself.
## Working-capital signals
These are year-over-year growth gaps against like-for-like quarterly revenue. Receivables and inventory are ending balances, whereas revenue is a quarterly flow.
| Quarter end | Receivables growth minus revenue growth | Inventory growth minus revenue growth |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2024-06-30 | 15.4% | -16.9% |
| 2024-09-30 | 7.89% | -9.07% |
| 2024-12-31 | -4.37% | -7.80% |
| 2025-03-31 | 4.88% | 6.52% |
| 2025-06-30 | 1.26% | 6.36% |
| 2025-09-30 | 5.07% | 1.53% |
| 2025-12-31 | 8.51% | -1.61% |
| 2026-03-31 | 22.7% | -14.7% |
Receivables are the clear concern: they outgrew revenue in all but one comparable quarter, and the latest gap widened sharply. Inventory is not corroborating the deterioration; it grew slower than revenue in the latest two quarters and materially slower in the latest quarter.
## Position implication
AMZN is currently 7.03% of the portfolio, worth $756K, and ranks 7th among 10 holdings by weight. Its weight has already declined by -0.04% since the prior run.
That is not an oversized position relative to the mandate:
- Issuer warning tier: 15.0%, with 7.97% or $856K of room.
- Issuer breach tier: 20.0%, with 13.0% or $1.39M of room.
- Amazon is the portfolio’s only Consumer Discretionary holding, so the sector exposure is also 7.03% and has the same concentration room.
**Reading for the book:** keep the position at roughly its present size rather than adding on the strength of reported earnings. The evidence does not yet justify a forced reduction: most quarters remain strongly cash-backed, inventory is improving, and AMZN is well inside both issuer and sector tiers. A second like-for-like quarter of sub-full cash conversion, positive accruals, and receivables materially outrunning revenue would change the reading toward trimming. Conversely, restored cash conversion and normalization of receivables growth would make the latest quarter look seasonal rather than structural.

{"text": "## Bottom line

Amazon’s earnings quality shows a **recent deterioration signal, but not yet a sustained decline**. The latest quarter combines weaker cash conversion, a mildly positive accruals ratio, and sharply faster receivables growth. However, the preceding quarter was exceptionally cash-generative, inventory growth has improved, and the eight-quarter history remains broadly cash-backed.

## Cash flow versus earnings

| Quarter end | Operating cash flow | Net income | Cash conversion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024-06-30 | $25.28B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2024-06-30] | $13.48B [f_6dc6feb54381@2024-06-30] | 187.5% [f_100c4db67295@2024-06-30] |
| 2024-09-30 | $25.97B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2024-09-30] | $15.33B [f_6dc6feb54381@2024-09-30] | 169.4% [f_100c4db67295@2024-09-30] |
| 2024-12-31 | $45.64B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2024-12-31] | $20.00B [f_6dc6feb54381@2024-12-31] | 228.1% [f_100c4db67295@2024-12-31] |
| 2025-03-31 | $17.02B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2025-03-31] | $17.13B [f_6dc6feb54381@2025-03-31] | 99.3% [f_100c4db67295@2025-03-31] |
| 2025-06-30 | $32.52B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2025-06-30] | $18.16B [f_6dc6feb54381@2025-06-30] | 179.0% [f_100c4db67295@2025-06-30] |
| 2025-09-30 | $35.52B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2025-09-30] | $21.19B [f_6dc6feb54381@2025-09-30] | 167.7% [f_100c4db67295@2025-09-30] |
| 2025-12-31 | $54.46B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2025-12-31] | $21.19B [f_6dc6feb54381@2025-12-31] | 257.0% [f_100c4db67295@2025-12-31] |
| 2026-03-31 | $26.03B [f_5bb736c6bc69@2026-03-31] | $30.25B [f_6dc6feb54381@2026-03-31] | 86.0% [f_100c4db67295@2026-03-31] |

Cash exceeded earnings in most quarters. The concern is that the latest conversion dropped below full coverage, versus 99.3% [f_100c4db67295@2025-03-31] in the same quarter a year earlier. Quarterly cash flow is seasonal, so the latest reading should not be extrapolated alone.

## Accruals trend

The sequence was:

- -2.13% [f_8e73fde81123@2024-06-30]
- -1.82% [f_8e73fde81123@2024-09-30]
- -4.10% [f_8e73fde81123@2024-12-31]
- 0.02% [f_8e73fde81123@2025-03-31]
- -2.10% [f_8e73fde81123@2025-06-30]
- -1.97% [f_8e73fde81123@2025-09-30]
- -4.07% [f_8e73fde81123@2025-12-31]
- 0.46% [f_8e73fde81123@2026-03-31]

The pattern is seasonal and broadly stable across like quarters, but the latest 0.46% [f_8e73fde81123@2026-03-31] is less favorable than 0.02% [f_8e73fde81123@2025-03-31]. That supports a deterioration flag, though its small magnitude does not indicate a broad accrual problem by itself.

## Working-capital signals

These are year-over-year growth gaps against like-for-like quarterly revenue. Receivables and inventory are ending balances, whereas revenue is a quarterly flow.

| Quarter end | Receivables growth minus revenue growth | Inventory growth minus revenue growth |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2024-06-30 | 15.4% [f_f28050254915@2024-06-30] | -16.9% [f_52a9158d3dde@2024-06-30] |
| 2024-09-30 | 7.89% [f_f28050254915@2024-09-30] | -9.07% [f_52a9158d3dde@2024-09-30] |
| 2024-12-31 | -4.37% [f_f28050254915@2024-12-31] | -7.80% [f_52a9158d3dde@2024-12-31] |
| 2025-03-31 | 4.88% [f_f28050254915@2025-03-31] | 6.52% [f_52a9158d3dde@2025-03-31] |
| 2025-06-30 | 1.26% [f_f28050254915@2025-06-30] | 6.36% [f_52a9158d3dde@2025-06-30] |
| 2025-09-30 | 5.07% [f_f28050254915@2025-09-30] | 1.53% [f_52a9158d3dde@2025-09-30] |
| 2025-12-31 | 8.51% [f_f28050254915@2025-12-31] | -1.61% [f_52a9158d3dde@2025-12-31] |
| 2026-03-31 | 22.7% [f_f28050254915@2026-03-31] | -14.7% [f_52a9158d3dde@2026-03-31] |

Receivables are the clear concern: they outgrew revenue in all but one comparable quarter, and the latest gap widened sharply. Inventory is not corroborating the deterioration; it grew slower than revenue in the latest two quarters and materially slower in the latest quarter.

turns.q: How much room does Exxon have if oil falls? Give net debt to EBITDA, EBIT interest coverage and FCF to debt for the latest four quarters against the same four a year earlier, read what the 10-K says about debt maturities and floating-rate exposure, and relate that to our XOM weight and the book's beta to USO.
turns.answer:
Exxon still has substantial balance-sheet room if oil falls, although its cash cushion and free-cash-flow debt coverage weakened year over year.
- **Net debt/EBITDA:** -0.02× for FY2025 versus -0.25× in FY2024. It remained modestly net-cash, but cash and equivalents fell to $10.68B from $23.03B.
- **EBIT interest coverage:** 67.91×, improving from 48.68×.
- **FCF/debt:** 254.0%, down materially from 619.9%, but still indicating annual free cash flow substantially exceeded debt.
These are annual four-quarter periods through FY2025 and FY2024, not trailing four quarters through 2026-03-31.
The maturity profile does not suggest an immediate refinancing wall. The 10-K says: “These amounts exclude that portion of long-term debt, totaling $6.2 billion, which matures within one year and is included in current liabilities. The amounts of long-term debt, excluding finance lease obligations, maturing in each of the four years after December 31, 2026, are: 2027 – $2.5 billion; 2028 – $1.7 billion; 2029 – $1.7 billion; and 2030 – $5.3 billion.” The schedule excludes finance leases.
On floating-rate exposure, Exxon describes fixed-for-floating swaps used to hedge certain fixed-rate debt, with settlements aligned to the debt’s interest payments. It says the fair-value changes offset and that: “This program was not material to the Consolidated Financial Statements.” That argues against floating-rate exposure being a major near-term vulnerability.
For the book, XOM is 4.61%, worth $496K, on the latest portfolio run dated 2026-09-10. This makes an oil downturn meaningful but not dominant at the single-name level. Exxon’s low leverage and very high coverage provide company-level absorption capacity, though the deterioration in cash and FCF/debt means less room than a year earlier.
The book’s standalone beta to USO cannot be quoted: the latest factor fit was collinear, so the USO leg was not independently determined. The fit used 750 sessions and 750 observations, with maximum VIF of 16.55× and R² of 80.7%. Therefore, I would not translate an oil-price decline into a book-level return from this run. A redesigned non-collinear exposure run would change that limitation; materially weaker free cash flow, loss of the net-cash position, or a larger XOM weight would make the downside reading less comfortable.

{"text": "Exxon still has substantial balance-sheet room if oil falls, although its cash cushion and free-cash-flow debt coverage weakened year over year.

- **Net debt/EBITDA:** -0.02× [f_4dbdf06e532e] for FY2025 versus -0.25× [f_7551ca3c8580] in FY2024. It remained modestly net-cash, but cash and equivalents fell to $10.68B [f_574845d0aee5] from $23.03B [f_75c9f6b9e076].
- **EBIT interest coverage:** 67.91× [f_bfde4112cdcb], improving from 48.68× [f_93b6b7cba865].
- **FCF/debt:** 254.0% [f_e7782f831f53], down materially from 619.9% [f_1777ee03550f], but still indicating annual free cash flow substantially exceeded debt.

These are annual four-quarter periods through FY2025 and FY2024, not trailing four quarters through 2026-03-31.

The maturity profile does not suggest an immediate refinancing wall. The 10-K says: “These amounts exclude that portion of long-term debt, totaling $6.2 billion, which matures within one year and is included in current liabilities. The amounts of long-term debt, excluding finance lease obligations, maturing in each of the four years after December 31, 2026, are: 2027 – $2.5 billion; 2028 – $1.7 billion; 2029 – $1.7 billion; and 2030 – $5.3 billion.” [f_7148ce7d05c9] The schedule excludes finance leases.

On floating-rate exposure, Exxon describes fixed-for-floating swaps used to hedge certain fixed-rate debt, with settlements aligned to the debt’s interest payments. It says the fair-value changes offset and that: “This program was not material to the Consolidated Financial Statements.” [f_ae1191ad990d] That argues against floating-rate exposure being a major near-term vulnerability.

For the book, XOM is 4.61% [f_a0dcbb812826], worth $496K [f_1ebd3eba01d8], on the latest run; those run figures are dated 2026-09-10, while the underlying positions are dated 2026-07-23. This makes an oil downturn meaningful but not dominant at the single-name level. Exxon’s low leverage and very high coverage provide company-level absorption capacity, though the deterioration in cash and FCF/debt means less room than a year earlier.

The book’s standalone beta to USO cannot be quoted: the latest factor fit was collinear, so the USO leg was not independently determined. The fit used 750 [f_bb5e953d3663] sessions and 750 [f_1a6750e03365] observations, with maximum VIF of 16.55× [f_4049d537a5fe] and R² of 80.7% [f_dcaea88cab09]. Therefore, I would not translate an oil-price decline into a book-level return from this run. A redesigned non-collinear exposure run would change that limitation; materially weaker free cash flow, loss of the net-cash position, or a larger XOM weight would make the downside reading less comfortable."}

turns.q: Where does NVIDIA's cash go? Capex, buybacks, dividends and SBC over the trailing twelve months, each as a share of operating cash flow, how each share has moved over three years, and whether the filing states how much buyback authorization remains.
turns.answer:
For the latest annual trailing-12-month period ending January 25, 2026, NVIDIA generated $103B of operating cash flow:
- **Buybacks:** $40.09B, or 39.0% of operating cash flow.
- **SBC:** $6.39B, or 6.22%. SBC is non-cash compensation, so this is a scale comparison rather than a cash use.
- **Capex:** $6.04B, or 5.88%.
- **Dividends:** $974M, or 0.95%.
**Three-year movement**—annual periods ending January 28, 2024, January 26, 2025, and January 25, 2026:
- **Capex:** 3.81% → 5.05% → 5.88%.
- **Buybacks:** 33.9% → 52.6% → 39.0%.
- **Dividends:** 1.41% → 1.30% → 0.95%.
- **SBC:** 12.6% → 7.39% → 6.22%.
The picture is buyback-heavy: repurchases remain by far the largest cash allocation, though their share fell from the prior-year peak. Capex’s share has risen steadily, while dividends and SBC have declined relative to operating cash generation.
The latest 10-Q says: “As of July 26, 2026, we were authorized, subject to certain specifications, to repurchase up to $99.3 billion of our common stock.” The filing describes this as authorization “up to” that amount rather than explicitly calling it the remaining authorization.
The three-year ratios are annual-period readings and do not incorporate subsequent quarterly results.

turns.answer:
The desk cannot produce the requested twelve-quarter gross, operating and net margin table. Lilly’s filed series lacks the period inputs needed for gross and operating margins, so the gross-to-operating gap is also unavailable. The desk returned annual—not quarterly—net margins, which I would not substitute for your requested series.
**What can be said now:** the latest filing shows gross margin at 81.9% in Q1 2026 versus 82.5% in Q1 2025. Lilly attributed that 0.6-point decline primarily to lower realized prices. That makes **pricing the clearest immediate driver**, not favorable costs. The available evidence does not separately quantify product mix, so it does not support calling the broader margin expansion mix-led. This reading applies only to Q1 2026 versus Q1 2025, not the full twelve-quarter period.
The latest Item 7 covers the annual 2025-versus-2024 change and refers readers to the prior filing for 2024 versus 2023; it does not provide a twelve-quarter bridge. The only usable longer-run profitability evidence is annual net margin: 19.7%, 21.9%, 15.4%, 23.5%, and 31.7%. These annual readings show substantial net-margin expansion after 2023, but they do not identify how much came from pricing, mix or costs.
Merck was not prepared on the desk, so readiness has now been initiated. It runs in the background and did not make Merck’s figures available this turn. Accordingly, there is no defensible matched-quarter comparison yet; Lilly’s gross and operating series are also currently unmeasured. Once Merck is ready, the comparison should be rerun on aligned quarter ends rather than using annual or nearby figures.

{"text": "Apple does not numerically rank its risks, so “biggest” is a qualitative reading of its latest disclosures. The principal themes are:

- **Competition and product execution:** rapid innovation, successful product transitions, and pressure from competitors.
- **Supply chain concentration:** reliance on outsourced manufacturing and single-source components.
- **Regulation:** expanding regulation, investigations, and potential penalties.
- **Product and AI risk:** the latest 10-Q adds emphasis on design or manufacturing defects and AI-related safety, cybersecurity, and online-safety obligations. It warns that AI can expose users to “harmful, inaccurate or other negative content and experiences” [f_41402f67f662].

The latest 10-Q says there were no material changes from the 2025 10-K risk factors except for its stated updates.

**Product concentration:** For the six months ended March 28, 2026, Apple reported iPhone revenue of $142,263 million [f_727421a3e89f], Services of $60,989 million [f_727421a3e89f], Wearables, Home and Accessories of $19,394 million [f_727421a3e89f], Mac of $16,785 million [f_727421a3e89f], and iPad of $15,509 million [f_727421a3e89f], against total net sales of $254,940 million [f_727421a3e89f]. This shows that iPhone remains the dominant product category, with Services a substantial second pillar.

**Geographic concentration:** For the same six-month period, revenue was Americas $103,622 million [f_7cc5adfb098f], Europe $66,201 million [f_7cc5adfb098f], Greater China $46,023 million [f_7cc5adfb098f], Rest of Asia Pacific $21,280 million [f_7cc5adfb098f], and Japan $17,814 million [f_7cc5adfb098f], totaling $254,940 million [f_7cc5adfb098f]. The exposure is led by the Americas, followed by Europe and Greater China.

The desk **does not hold product or geographic revenue as structured figures**; these amounts come from filing-text tables. turns.answer:
**Bottom line:** the desk cannot establish whether the market treats JPMorgan as riskier than it did twelve months ago. Its price tools only calculate latest-window readings and cannot recreate the same indicators as of a historical date. The current signals themselves do not look especially stressed, but they are not a valid year-over-year comparison.
**Current market readings, through 2026-09-10**
- Thirty-session volatility: 14.2%.
- Beta to SPY: 0.78×, measured over the latest one-year window.
- Distance from the 52-week high: -3.18%, using the desk’s signed convention.
Those readings show below-market sensitivity and a price close to its annual high. But they describe market behavior—not investor intent—and cannot answer “riskier than a year ago” without comparable readings as of 2025-09-10. The desk’s historical-date request failed because its price methods do not accept an as-of date: “run(): the program did not run: every node with a type problem is listed with its fix; nodes that depend on one are not repeated — historical_vol_30: price.volatility: params do not fit the method's schema; historical_beta_spy: price.beta: params do not fit the method's schema; historical_from_high: price.distance_from_52w_high: params do not fit the method's schema”.
**Interest expense**
The filed series ends before the latest three fiscal years, so the desk returned 2021–2023 rather than estimating later values:
- 2021: $5.55B.
- 2022: $26.10B, up 370.0%.
- 2023: $81.32B, up 211.6%.
For a bank, that sharp increase should not be read like rising debt-service pressure at an industrial issuer: interest expense is an operating cost of gathering and using funding.
**Pretax-to-net-income gap**
- FY2023: pretax income $61.61B; net income $49.55B; gap $12.06B, equal to 19.6% of pretax income.
- FY2024: pretax income $75.08B; net income $58.47B; gap $16.61B, or 22.1%. The gap widened 37.7%.
- FY2025: pretax income $72.59B; net income $57.05B; gap $15.55B, or 21.4%. The gap narrowed -6.40%.
This is an earnings-conversion residual—principally taxes and any filed income-attribution difference—not a separately reported expense. Its modest narrowing in FY2025 does not, by itself, suggest worsening conversion risk.
**Bank-method boundary**
The desk does not apply industrial-company leverage and coverage measures to JPM, including total debt, net debt, debt/EBITDA, net debt/EBITDA, debt/operating cash flow, FCF/debt, or EBIT/interest coverage. Current and quick ratios also do not apply. Nor do conventional gross, operating, and net margins, free cash flow, ROIC, or working-capital-cycle measures.
**What would change the reading:** comparable 2025-09-10 snapshots showing higher current volatility and beta, together with a materially greater distance below the annual high, would support “riskier than a year ago.” The desk cannot currently produce those historical snapshots, so the defensible conclusion is **not demonstrated**, rather than yes or no.

{"text": "**Bottom line:** the desk cannot establish whether the market treats JPMorgan as riskier than it did twelve months ago. Its price tools only calculate latest-window readings and cannot recreate the same indicators as of a historical date. The current signals themselves do not look especially stressed, but they are not a valid year-over-year comparison.

**Current market readings, through 2026-09-10**

- Thirty-session volatility: 14.2% [f_4995c732bbf0].
- Beta to SPY: 0.78× [f_95d4a8a2b283], measured over the latest one-year window.
- Distance from the 52-week high: -3.18% [f_54129991c370], using the desk’s signed convention.

Those readings show below-market sensitivity and a price close to its annual high. But they describe market behavior—not investor intent—and cannot answer “riskier than a year ago” without comparable readings as of 2025-09-10. The desk’s historical-date request failed because its price methods do not accept an as-of date: “run(): the program did not run: every node with a type problem is listed with its fix; nodes that depend on one are not repeated — historical_vol_30: price.volatility: params do not fit the method's schema; historical_beta_spy: price.beta: params do not fit the method's schema; historical_from_high: price.distance_from_52w_high: params do not fit the method's schema” [f_b9f24b539003].

**Interest expense**

The filed series ends before the latest three fiscal years, so the desk returned 2021–2023 rather than estimating later values:

- 2021: $5.55B [f_9810b82a7d82@2021-12-31].
- 2022: $26.10B [f_9810b82a7d82@2022-12-31], up 370.0% [f_6140a7df0216@2022-12-31].
- 2023: $81.32B [f_9810b82a7d82@2023-12-31], up 211.6% [f_6140a7df0216@2023-12-31].

For a bank, that sharp increase should not be read like rising debt-service pressure at an industrial issuer: interest expense is an operating cost of gathering and using funding.

**Pretax-to-net-income gap**

- FY2023: pretax income $61.61B [f_188c3287a0b2@2023-12-31]; net income $49.55B [f_41fe2d165896@2023-12-31]; gap $12.06B [f_01cbda50e179@2023-12-31], equal to 19.6% [f_befe10f921ad@2023-12-31] of pretax income.
- FY2024: pretax income $75.08B [f_188c3287a0b2@2024-12-31]; net income $58.47B [f_41fe2d165896@2024-12-31]; gap $16.61B [f_01cbda50e179@2024-12-31], or 22.1% [f_befe10f921ad@2024-12-31]. The gap widened 37.7% [f_7ed03a269280@2024-12-31].
- FY2025: pretax income $72.59B [f_188c3287a0b2@2025-12-31]; net income $57.05B [f_41fe2d165896@2025-12-31]; gap $15.55B [f_01cbda50e179@2025-12-31], or 21.4% [f_befe10f921ad@2025-12-31]. The gap narrowed -6.40% [f_7ed03a269280@2025-12-31].

This is an earnings-conversion residual—principally taxes and any filed income-attribution difference—not a separately reported expense. Its modest narrowing in FY2025 does not, by itself, suggest worsening conversion risk.

**Bank-method boundary**

The desk does not apply industrial-company leverage and coverage measures to JPM, including total debt [f_186ba6bd2ae6], net debt [f_07fcec0221a1], debt/EBITDA [f_574946c05c6e], net debt/EBITDA [f_8ca835d4a2f3], debt/operating cash flow [f_441a7bb79e86], FCF/debt [f_0cf433ba6ce8], or EBIT/interest coverage [f_63cb6588f68e]. Current and quick ratios also do not apply [f_485bb21ccaae] [f_598bc309121c]. Nor do conventional gross, operating, and net margins [f_573e0f4d14f0] [f_6404b6f2bf97] [f_6cb61bc0c7d4], free cash flow [f_7477272efdb0], ROIC [f_13b1d7febba7], or working-capital-cycle measures [f_0af4173b5894].

**What would change the reading:** comparable 2025-09-10 snapshots showing higher current volatility and beta, together with a materially greater distance below the annual high, would support “riskier than a year ago.” The desk cannot currently produce those historical snapshots, so the defensible conclusion is **not demonstrated**, rather than yes or no."}

turns.q: Compare the capex intensity and ROIC of Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon over the last three fiscal years. Who spends the most relative to revenue and earns the least on it, and how does that sit with the book's exposure to QQQ?
turns.answer:
Fiscal years are not perfectly calendar-aligned: Microsoft’s year ends June 30; Alphabet’s and Amazon’s fiscal years end in December.
| Issuer | Capex intensity FY2023 / FY2024 / FY2025 | ROIC FY2023 / FY2024 / FY2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | 13.3% / 18.1% / 22.9% | 32.8% / 29.7% / 29.7% |
| Alphabet | 10.5% / 15.0% / 22.7% | 26.6% / 29.7% / 24.8% |
| Amazon | 9.17% / 13.0% / 18.4% | 15.2% / 22.3% / 16.2% |
**Reading:** Microsoft spends the most relative to revenue—it ranked first in all three years—but it does **not** earn the least. Its latest ROIC is the highest at 29.7%. Amazon earns the least, at 16.2%, and its latest capex intensity is also the lowest at 18.4%. Alphabet is the key watchpoint: its latest capex intensity is 22.7%, just behind Microsoft, while its latest ROIC is 24.8%, below Microsoft.
**Portfolio implication:** The premise of QQQ exposure needs correcting. The book does not directly hold QQQ, and the desk does not produce a standalone QQQ sensitivity because its book-level factor legs are collinear. Instead, exposure is direct: Microsoft is 16.0%, Alphabet 12.4%, and Amazon 7.03%, totaling 35.5%. That combined weight was also 35.5% in the prior run, with a -0.05% change.
So the book has a substantial direct concentration in the same large growth issuers commonly associated with QQQ, but it should not be called measured QQQ exposure. The main fundamental watchpoint is Alphabet’s convergence toward Microsoft-level spending without Microsoft-level ROIC; Amazon remains the lowest-return name, while Microsoft’s heavy spending is currently supported by the strongest return.

turns.q: Has Microsoft's leverage story changed? Total debt, net debt and net debt to EBITDA at each of the last five fiscal year-ends, interest coverage, and what the latest 10-K says about commercial paper. Then: if rates rose 100bp, what does the rates_shock_up scenario say happens to the book?
turns.answer:
Microsoft’s leverage story looks broadly stable-to-improving, but the requested five-year debt series cannot be completed from validated desk data.
- **2021-06-30:** Total debt and net debt unavailable; net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 31.31×.
- **2022-06-30:** Total debt and net debt unavailable; net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 41.58×.
- **2023-06-30:** Total debt was $47.24B; net debt was $12.53B. Net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 46.38×.
- **2024-06-30:** Total debt was $51.63B; net debt was $33.31B. Net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 37.72×.
- **2025-06-30:** Total debt was $43.15B; net debt was $12.91B. Net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 52.84×.
The desk cannot calculate net debt/EBITDA because the required depreciation-and-amortization input is missing. It also cannot validate 2021–2022 total and net debt because commercial paper was not reported or reachable at those year-ends; it will not label an understated partial sum as total debt. The 2025 coverage reading substitutes the reported non-operating interest line because the former interest-expense tagging ends after 2024.
**Interpretation:** Debt and net debt rose in 2024, then reversed sharply in 2025, while coverage reached the strongest reading in this five-year series. That supports a temporary 2024 balance-sheet expansion rather than a lasting deterioration. The reading would change if the missing historical debt components or EBITDA inputs showed materially worse leverage, or if coverage weakened persistently rather than rebounding.
**Commercial paper:** In Item 8 of the latest 10-K, Microsoft says the paper had an “interest rate of 5.4% and maturities ranging from 28 days to 152 days. The estimated fair value of this commercial paper approximates its carrying value.”
**100bp rates rise:** The latest portfolio run contains no figure under the requested `rates_shock_up` scenario: “rates_up was not computed — unknown_name: run_e2945c5ebd5a holds no figure named 'scenarios.rates_up'.” Accordingly, the desk cannot state a measured book gain or loss from a 100bp rise. It also withholds stress-loss results pending validation. Mandate scenarios can reprice holdings and rerun checks, but they do not refit betas or volatility or recalculate VaR or stress losses. A validated scenario identifier or explicit trade instructions would be needed to change that conclusion.

{"text": "Microsoft’s leverage story looks broadly stable-to-improving, but the requested five-year debt series cannot be completed from validated desk data.

- **2021-06-30:** Total debt and net debt unavailable; net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 31.31× [f_dfbe8fdaccdc@2021-06-30].
- **2022-06-30:** Total debt and net debt unavailable; net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 41.58× [f_dfbe8fdaccdc@2022-06-30].
- **2023-06-30:** Total debt was $47.24B [f_5e467b3234dd]; net debt was $12.53B [f_3024aab448c0]. Net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 46.38× [f_dfbe8fdaccdc@2023-06-30].
- **2024-06-30:** Total debt was $51.63B [f_6deaa5731a8e]; net debt was $33.31B [f_ca92ff86657a]. Net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 37.72× [f_dfbe8fdaccdc@2024-06-30].
- **2025-06-30:** Total debt was $43.15B [f_ab545fff7f2a]; net debt was $12.91B [f_32bb7579eb6d]. Net debt/EBITDA unavailable. Interest coverage was 52.84× [f_dfbe8fdaccdc@2025-06-30].

The desk cannot calculate net debt/EBITDA because the required depreciation-and-amortization input is missing. It also cannot validate 2021–2022 total and net debt because commercial paper was not reported or reachable at those year-ends; it will not label an understated partial sum as total debt. The 2025 coverage reading substitutes the reported non-operating interest line because the former interest-expense tagging ends after 2024.

**Interpretation:** Debt and net debt rose in 2024, then reversed sharply in 2025, while coverage reached the strongest reading in this five-year series. That supports a temporary 2024 balance-sheet expansion rather than a lasting deterioration. The reading would change if the missing historical debt components or EBITDA inputs showed materially worse leverage, or if coverage weakened persistently rather than rebounding.

**Commercial paper:** In Item 8 of the latest 10-K, Microsoft says the paper had an “interest rate of 5.4% and maturities ranging from 28 days to 152 days. The estimated fair value of this commercial paper approximates its carrying value.” [f_6b1aa79d8dab]

**100bp rates rise:** The latest portfolio run contains no figure under the requested `rates_shock_up` scenario: “rates_up was not computed — unknown_name: run_e2945c5ebd5a holds no figure named 'scenarios.rates_up'.” [f_00a68bd347c3] Accordingly, the desk cannot state a measured book gain or loss from a 100bp rise. turns.q: How liquid is the book? For each holding, position value against 20-day average dollar volume, days to liquidate at 20% of ADV, which names take longest, and whether those are the same names sitting near their issuer limits.
turns.answer:
The book is highly liquid on exchange-traded volume. Using the latest 20-session window ending 2026-09-10 and a 20% participation rate:
| Holding | Position value | 20-day average dollar volume | Days to liquidate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| JPM | $1.59M | $1.98B/day | 0.0040 |
| LLY | $1.35M | $2.94B/day | 0.0023 |
| HYG | $786K | $2.56B/day | 0.0015 |
| TLT | $646K | $2.48B/day | 0.0013 |
| XOM | $496K | $2.24B/day | 0.0011 |
| GOOGL | $1.33M | $7.70B/day | 0.0009 |
| MSFT | $1.72M | $10.51B/day | 0.0008 |
| AAPL | $1.63M | $13.27B/day | 0.0006 |
| AMZN | $756K | $8.37B/day | 0.0005 |
| NVDA | $437K | $28.29B/day | 0.0001 |
The table is ordered from longest to shortest liquidation time. JPM is slowest, followed by LLY, HYG, TLT, and XOM. Even JPM requires only 0.0040 days under the stated assumption. Every position is below its one-day capacity; the summed holding value is $10.75M, equal to 100.0% of portfolio value.
**Overlap with issuer-limit pressure is partial, not complete.**
- LLY is already beyond its issuer warning tier by -0.54%, while JPM has only 0.19% remaining.
- HYG, TLT, and XOM are slower in liquidity rank but have substantially more warning room: 7.68%, 8.99%, and 10.4%.
- The other names already beyond warning—MSFT at -1.04% and AAPL at -0.20%—are among the faster names to liquidate.
- No holding is at or beyond its breach tier.
**Implication:** liquidity is not presently the constraint. The key concentration-management names are MSFT, LLY, AAPL, and JPM; LLY and JPM deserve the most attention because they combine relatively tighter issuer-limit room with the longest liquidation times, although those times remain negligible at current market volume.
HYG and TLT use ETF trading volume only; this does not assess liquidity of their underlying holdings. Position values and the 20-session trading-volume window are dated 2026-09-10.

turns.q: Anything in the last two weeks that touches something we hold? Search for material news on our top five by weight, and for each say whether the price already moved: ten-day window return against SPY and distance from the 52-week high.
turns.answer:
I screened the latest run’s top five holdings by weight. The news search covers the last two weeks through today, but price data only run through 2026-09-10; the ten-session return window is 2026-08-27 through 2026-09-10. Therefore, post-window news is not captured in these returns.
- **MSFT — 16.0%.** No material operating development found; a September 9 proxy-solicitation filing was excluded as non-material. MSFT returned -2.50% over ten sessions, trailing SPY by -0.78%, and MSFT stood -8.41% below its 52-week high. Without a material item, this is general price weakness rather than evidence that specific news was absorbed.
- **AAPL — 15.2%.** On “2026/09/14”, Apple sought expedited discovery into OpenAI ahead of an October 1 injunction hearing, seeking evidence that allegedly confidential information entered OpenAI’s unreleased consumer device. Through September 10, AAPL returned 3.81%, outperforming SPY by 5.53%, and AAPL stood -3.89% from its high. **Not captured:** the item arrived after the price window.
- **JPM — 14.8%.** No material issuer development found; routine structured-note issuance and an insider sale were excluded. JPM returned -0.19%, outperforming SPY by 1.53%, and JPM stood -3.18% from its high. Again, that is general context, not a news reaction.
- **LLY — 12.5%.** AtaiBeckley shareholders approved its merger agreement with Lilly at a meeting “held on September 8, 2026”, advancing Lilly’s planned expansion into treatment-resistant depression and other mental-health therapies. LLY returned -4.51%, underperforming SPY by -2.79%, and LLY stood -12.3% from its high. **Only partly informative:** the event occurred near the end of the return window, and approval timing is not necessarily publication timing; the move cannot be attributed to it from these data alone.
- **GOOGL — 12.4%.** A ruling reported “Sept 2” allowed Google to avoid a forced sale of its ad-tech business, reducing breakup risk, though behavioral remedies remain. GOOGL returned -2.30%, trailing SPY by -0.58%, and GOOGL stood -17.3% below its high. **The window includes the report date, but there is no clear positive repricing:** GOOGL still underperformed SPY and remains well below its high.
**Book implication:** AAPL’s litigation item is the clearest unmeasured development because it postdates the available prices. GOOGL’s favorable ruling overlapped the window without visible relative strength, while LLY showed the weakest relative move but its event timing does not support causal attribution. A fresh price window would be needed to assess whether AAPL’s September 14 news has since been absorbed.

turns.q: What share of Amazon's revenue is AWS, how has that share moved over three years, and how much of our AMZN return over the last year relative to SPY does that explain?
turns.answer:
AWS’s share of Amazon consolidated revenue rose steadily:
- 2023: 15.8%
- 2024: 16.9%
- 2025: 18.0%
That is an increase of 2.17% from 2023 to 2025—this desk output is labeled as a percent, but it represents a percentage-point change. These calculations use filing-table amounts in millions and the displayed shares are rounded.
Over the latest one-year window, from 2025-09-10 through 2026-09-10, AMZN returned 9.36%, versus 17.5% for SPY, an underperformance of -8.12%. All returns use adjusted closes through the latest available session.
We cannot quantify how much of that relative return AWS’s rising revenue share explains. The evidence establishes a business-mix shift and coincident stock underperformance, not causation or return attribution by segment. For this holding, the defensible reading is therefore: AWS became more important to Amazon’s revenue, but that shift did not translate into AMZN outperforming SPY over the measured year. A causal reading would require segment-level expectations and valuation or event attribution that the desk does not hold.

turns.q: Will Lilly's margins keep expanding next year?
turns.answer:
The desk does not forecast, so it cannot say whether Lilly’s margins will keep expanding next year.
The latest evidence is mixed rather than clearly supportive:
- Lilly attributed its recent gross-margin contraction primarily to lower realized prices. Because gross profit is unavailable as a computable filed line, this direction comes from management’s filing discussion.
- Below gross profit, R&D rose 28% and marketing, selling and administrative expense rose 19%, while acquired IPR&D fell 63%. Acquired IPR&D is transaction- and milestone-driven, so that decline is not a dependable recurring cost benefit.
- A measured operating-margin bridge is unavailable because Lilly does not provide the required operating-income series in the desk’s filed data.
**Bottom line:** continued expansion is not established. The reading would improve if product mix and production efficiencies more than offset realized-price pressure and rising recurring operating costs. It would weaken if price pressure persists or R&D and selling costs continue to outgrow revenue.
